What is it? A connected set of three 15.6-inch HD screens that create a multi-monitor setup for your MacBook.
Who is it for? People on the look out for easily packed-up but greatly expanded screen space, and for whom a single MacBook display means constantly shuffling windows. This is a good solution for hot-desking, moving between rooms, and temporary workspaces.
Who shouldn’t buy it? Travelers looking for a backpack-able portable monitor, cafe-based workers, or one-desk workers happy to keep their displays always set up.
A MacBook encompassing computer, keyboard and trackpad (as well as webcam, microphone and speakers) is a formidable tool but many of us use it more like a desktop most of the time: connected to one or more static external displays, and maybe a docking station to add ports and more.
The KYY X90G Quad Portable Monitor sidesteps the standard desktop monitor model to instead create a super-laptop with three extra screens—one on either side and one above your open MacBook.
How many extra screens does the KYY X90G add?
KYY is counting the MacBook’s built-in screen in its quad lineup. The three it adds are larger than most we’ve seen of this type, with 15.6-inch screens larger than most MacBook screens, with the exception of the mighty 16-inch MacBook Pro.
The maximum resolution of each is 1920 x 1080 pixels (aka 1080p or Full HD) so some way off even the MacBook Neo’s 2408 x 1506 pixels, but still offering decent supplementary working spaces.

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




The screens fold up into a tidy but not insubstantial package measuring 15.4 x 8.9 x 1.3 inches (390 x 226 x 34mm) and weighing a hefty 6.4lbs (2.9kg).
In comparison, the two QHD-screen Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro measures 13.4 x 8.8 x 0.9 inches (34 x 22.4 x 2.3cm) folded up and weighs a more portable 4.13lbs (1.9kg). That makes it more carriable, but its 14-inch screens are smaller and fewer than what you get with the X90G.

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




Due to its collapsible form the X90G is a portable display, but it’s not an easy carry in your backpack. It’s fine for carrying between rooms or transporting by any means not on foot, which will suit you if you want to pack up your working space at the end of a working day or taking it on a long one-destination trip away from the office.
Hot-deskers with lockable cupboard space will find the X90G a handy display solution. If you prefer something more traditional, look to the larger but lower-footprint UPerfect Delta Max or Delta Mega that stack two screens on top of each other and fold away when you want a clear desk. For more options, read our reviews of the best portable displays for Mac.
It’s also something of a dragon when folded out to its full wingspan, measuring nearly 4 feet (1.2m) from one side to the other and a foot and a half (0.46m) vertically. You’ll likely get given a takeaway cup if you casually unfurl the KYY X90G in your local coffee shop.

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




Are the KYY X90G’s 1080p screens good enough?
Resolution: 1920 x 1080 pixels
Brightness: 350 nits
Contrast ratio: 1200:1
Aspect ratio: 16:9
Color gamut (NTSC): 85%
The brightness and contrast ratio of the X90G are impressive, but creatives will look askance at the 85% gamut for their color-critical work. It might not be for designers but as a productivity accessory it adds a lot of screen space—although at the expense of your desk space—that might be perfect for programmers, analysts, traders and remote workers, and people for whom a single 14- or 16-inch MacBook display means constantly shuffling windows.
At 15.6 inches, 1080p is fine for text and spreadsheets but not razor-sharp. 350 nits is respectable for a portable screen and fine indoors.
Does the KYY X90G put any weight on your MacBook?
Many portable multi-screen add-ons—usually just adding a screen either side of the MacBook’s own—clip or clamp onto the laptop’s display, which puts load on the hinge. The Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro, for example, works best with four heavy-duty magnets you need to place on your MacBook’s lid. The X90G avoids this with an integrated solid but flexible all-aluminum frame that supports the screens independently, so your MacBook lid carries none of the weight. Behind your MacBook the X90G’s backplate hosts a sturdy 90-degree stand.
The top screen auto-rotates when folded back, which allows you to position the X90G in some interesting formations. The build quality is impressive, and the hinges look robust.

				
					

				
			X90G’s Portrait mode features automatic orientation.
Simon Jary




The X90G supports Extended, Mirrored, Portrait, Presentation and Sharing modes. Mirroring and presentation are useful for face-to-face meetings, and portrait suits reading and coding. Extended mode is the main draw for most people, such as placing chat and notes on the left, reference docs on the right, and the browser or IDE on top.

				
					

				
			Angle one screen so the person sitting opposite can see your presentation.
Simon Jary




I found the top screen the most useful of the three. It’s closer to your eyeline than the side screens that instead work better for keeping less-used browser tabs and folders.
How easy is the KYY X90G to set up on a Mac?
The X90G uses one full-function USB-C port for video, plus a second power-only USB-C power port. A USB-A to USB-C adapter is included, which Mac users won’t need, and you might want to snip it off as this legacy connector just gets in the way.
As the displays take up to 30W of power itself we found we had to power both the X90G and our 14-inch MacBook Pro for the smoothest operation.
Three extra screens are beyond the functionality of most Macs, so you need to install third-party software, SiliconMotion’s InstantView. Installation is fairly painless and the manual gives you a step-by-step guide. The software comes on an included USB-C/USB-A memory stick.

				
					

				
			The X90G folds up into a tidy—if weighty—package.
Simon Jary




Unfolding the X90G’s screens is simple, but I did have to look hard at the installation one-pager to work out some of the folding techniques for portrait, sharing and presentation modes.
You’ll then need to enter your Mac’s System Settings>Displays to arrange the three screens and set resolutions—each screen can have its own independent resolution and orientation.
And each screen has its own On-Screen Display menu, allowing you to set Brightness, Backlight, Contrast, Sharpness, Color Temperature/Saturation, Language, and so on.
Is the KYY X90G worth $738.99?
The KYY X90G Quad Portable Monitor comes at a high price: $738.99 is an investment as hefty as the display itself, although at the time of writing it was selling on Amazon for around $400, so I’d look there first as that seems reasonable considering you’re getting a well-built collapsible three-screen setup.
U.K. customers can’t buy direct, which isn’t such a shame given the high direct price, and should check Amazon, too. 
Should you buy the KYY X90G Quad Portable Monitor?
Look elsewhere if you need professional color accuracy, high refresh rates, or retina sharpness, or if you work from one desk all the time—one or two large external displays will do better there (see best monitors for Mac), and a single portable monitor is simpler to carry and set up (see best portable monitors for Mac).
Its unwieldy shape and size might not be for everybody, but the well-built KYY X90G has a place in your life if you need multiple flexibly positioned HD monitors within easy sight that can be speedily collapsed and hidden away when you don’t need them anymore.

title: Manchester's Bee Card Now Fully Supported in Apple Wallet
content:
In August, Transport for Greater Manchester announced that the Bee Card could be added to the Apple Wallet app on the iPhone and Apple Watch, but it was limited to younger riders using free or discounted "Our Pass" tickets. As of this Tuesday, though, the Bee Card is now fully supported in Apple Wallet for all types of Bee Network tickets.


To add the card to Apple Wallet, open the app, tap on the plus sign in the top-right corner, select "Travel Card" (may appear as "Transit Card" for some users), scroll down to the United Kingdom section, and choose Bee Network.

Once the card has been added, you can buy bus and tram tickets directly in Apple Wallet and store them on the virtual Bee Card. Then, when traveling on the Bee Network in Greater Manchester, you can simply tap your iPhone or Apple Watch on a card reader to pay for your fare. If you enable Express Mode, there is no need to wake or unlock the iPhone or Apple Watch when holding it near the card reader.

What is it? A color-accurate 4K display with a highly adjustable stand that makes the Apple Studio Display look rather expensive.
Who is it for? Professional photo and video creators, plus gamers.
Who shouldn’t buy it? People for whom only the very sharpest text will do.
Buy the Asus if you want OLED, 120Hz, HDR, far more ports, adjustable stand, much lower price. 
Buy Apple’s Studio Display if you want: Sharper 5K text, better speakers, built-in webcam, stronger Mac integration.
Apple recently updated its Studio Display, and our reviewer wasn’t overly impressed with the barely new model, especially at such a high price. It’s still one of the best monitors you can buy for a Mac, but ASUS may now have made the better monitor—at a much more realistic price point.
That might sound like heresy when the two 27-inch displays are sitting side by side on the same desk. The 2026 Apple Studio Display is quintessentially Apple: beautifully integrated, razor-sharp, packed with decent speakers and a great camera for video calls. The ASUS ProArt Display OLED PA279CDV is less elegant (its plastic shell and bezels are no match for the Studio Display’s aluminum and full-face front glass panel), with basic speakers and no webcam, but technically more ambitious—and in several crucial ways, it is considerably more capable.

				
					

				
			The ASUS ProArt is happy in Portrait as well as Landscape orientation. If you want a more vertical view of the Studio Display Apple will make you swap the stand for a VESA mount adapter.
Simon Jary




Is 4K sharp enough compared with the Studio Display’s 5K?
Apple wins for text sharpness.
ASUS wins for motion, contrast, HDR and creative/video work.
Apple’s biggest weapon in the fight is its 5K Retina advantage. The Studio Display packs 5120 x 2880 pixels, giving it a wonderful 218ppi pixel density, ensuring that text is exceptionally crisp and the interfaces look beautifully rendered.
The ASUS is 4K, at 3840 x 2160, and 166ppi. That’s still sharp, but put the two displays side by side and the difference is clear, particularly with text—important for writers, developers and anyone who spends eight hours staring at browser windows, documents and menus, and those with the extra cash in their pocket.
If your workload is primarily Safari/Mail/Word/Excel/coding/lots of text, the Apple Studio Display has a meaningful advantage, but then we’d recommend you look at more affordable 5K displays such as the $999/£899 BenQ MA270S or BenQ PD2730S or budget $699 KTC 5K2K Monitor. Don’t get me wrong, the text on the PA279CDV is great—just not 5K great.
Read our reviews for more of the best monitors for Mac.
The ProArt’s secret weapon is sitting behind all those pixels: its QD-OLED panel gives the ASUS a huge advantage in contrast, with deep blacks, virtually instantaneous response times and much more convincing HDR. Its 120Hz refresh rate also makes scrolling, animations and timeline scrubbing noticeably smoother than the Apple’s 60Hz panel. If you’ve become accustomed to the 120Hz ProMotion display on a MacBook Pro, the Studio Display’s 60Hz refresh rate can feel like a step backwards. The ASUS doesn’t make that compromise. For photography and especially HDR video work, the PA279CDV is the display I’d want in front of me.
Color performance is strong on both. ASUS targets professional creators with factory calibration, a Delta E (ΔE) below 1.5 and broad DCI-P3 coverage, while Apple offers a range of color and reference modes. For HDR video and visually demanding creative work, though, the ASUS’s OLED panel is the more compelling choice.
The ProArt’s studio-grade 99% DCI-P3 gamut ensures rich, vivid colors, making it ideal for color-intensive projects. The peak brightness of 1000 nits allows for outstanding contrast between its deeper blacks and brighter whites.

				
					

				
			HDR and 120Hz refresh rate don’t go together on every resolution option, for example 2560 x 1440 pixels.
Simon Jary




Is the ASUS better for color, HDR and creative work?
Screen: 27-inch OLED
Finish: Gloss (anti-scratch)
Max resolution: 3840 x 2160 pixels
Refresh rate: 120Hz
DCI-P3 color coverage: 99%
sRGB color coverage: 100%
Contrast Ratio: True Black
Delta E (dE): <1.5
Brightness: 1,000 nits (peak)
OLED is the display technology for anyone who values image quality above all else. Its self-lit pixels deliver perfect blacks, exceptional contrast and near-instant response times, making HDR content, photos, video and games look spectacular. For creators and entertainment fans, OLED offers a richer, more immersive visual experience than IPS. If you spend most of your time on general productivity work, spend hours reading text, or work in brightly lit rooms, an IPS panel (and 5K if you can afford it) might make more sense.
ASUS employs OLED Care features to safeguard the display against image burn-in which can be a problem with OLED screens. This dynamically detects and identifies the task bar, logos, and video edges, reducing the brightness around them to minimise the risk of burn-in.
The peak brightness isn’t as stunning as on the Apple Studio Display XDR, but that costs around $3,000 compared to $699 for the ASUS. 

				
					

				
			Cable management on the multi-adjustable stand is basic but appreciated. 
Simon Jary




How adjustable is the ASUS ProArt stand?
Where Apple charges you an extra $400/£400 for its tilt and height-adjustable stand, this comes as standard with the ASUS ProArt, which offers tilt, swivel, 90° pivot, and 5-inch height adjustments for a more comfortable viewing experience. The small-footprint stand (shown above) also features basic built-in cable management, where cables can be passed neatly through an opening that should lead to a more organised workspace. To be fair to Apple, the Studio Display’s stand features the same, but some monitor stands don’t bother with this cable-clutter remover.
The monitor also tackles clutter by having a built-in power supply, so there’s no power brick sitting under your desk.
Does the ASUS have better connectivity than the Studio Display?
Where Apple sticks rigidly to its Thunderbolt/USB-C connectors—with the Studio Display offering two 80Gbps Thunderbolt 5 and two 10Gbps USB-C ports—the ASUS ProArt gives you HDMI 2.1, 2x DisplayPort (daisy-chainable in and out), 3x USB-C (max. 5Gbps), 3x USB-A ports, a headphone jack, and 96W MacBook passthrough charging. With a built-in KVM, it can happily sit between a MacBook and a Windows PC, sharing your keyboard and mouse between them.
Data transfer is weak compared to Apple’s Thunderbolt 5, but plenty for the video connection.

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




Apple’s approach is more prescriptive—it looks fantastic, but the ProArt behaves like a professional monitor rather than a beautifully packaged Mac peripheral.
Is the ASUS ProArt PA279CDV good value?
Comparing like for like with a decent tilt and height-adjustable stand included, the Apple Studio Display’s $1,899/£1,899 price tag looks painful next to the ASUS ProArt’s much more affordable $699 / £649—also available at Amazon and Amazon UK. That extra is a lot to pay for the Studio Display’s 5K resolution plus webcam and superior speakers. 
The ProArt’s speakers are pretty tinny, so you might want to invest $100-200 in better audio if using the screen for streaming or gaming. You’ll have change over to pick one of the best webcams for Mac we’ve reviewed to match the Apple Studio Display for video-call quality.
The more expensive ($899) Dell 32 Plus QD-OLED is similar except for its 31.6-inch size that gives you more screen space but a drop in sharpness.
Should you buy the ASUS ProArt Display OLED PA279CDV?
ASUS has put a lot of effort into optimizing the ProArt for Mac users, including intuitive controls such as MacBook Keyboard Sync and matching up color temperature with your MacBook, with the ASUS DisplayWidget Center for macOS.  
The Apple Studio Display remains the better choice if your priorities are razor-sharp text, great speakers, an excellent webcam, and effortless Mac integration. But the ASUS ProArt Display OLED PA279CDV is the more exciting display. 120Hz OLED, proper HDR, professional color, extensive connectivity and a genuinely adjustable stand make it hard to ignore—particularly for creative professionals.

Apple iPad mini A17 Pro
View Deal
If you’ve been delaying getting a new tablet because of Apple’s recent price hikes, Prime Day is the best time to take the leap. Apple’s iPad mini with an A17 Pro chip is on sale for $499 right now, a savings of $100 off its MSRP and bringing it back to its original price before the RAM surge.
The iPad mini brings you everything you want from an iPad just in a smaller size that actually fits in one hand, your purse, or a jacket pocket. It’s light enough to use for reading, comfortable enough to carry with you on a trip, and perfectly capable of handling a wide range of tasks. Do you need to send an email, stream a movie, or take on an unexpected work call — done. The 8.3-inch Liquid Retina display looks sharp and vibrant, and the A17 Pro chip keeps everything running fast and smooth. The iPad supports iOS 27 with the new Siri AI, all-day battery, a 12MP front camera with Center Stage, and Wi-Fi 6E as well.
You may have read rumors that a new model is on the way with a bunch of upgrades, including an OLED ProMotion display, new design, and an A20 Pro processor. That’s true, but we also think it’ll come with a price hike of at least $50, if not $100. Apple raised the prices of its latest iPhones and Macs without any major upgrades, so we think the new iPad mini could start at $699.
So go shell out $499 and grab this tablet with 128GB of storage space while it’s still on sale. Because it might be the lowest price you’ll ever be able to spend on a new iPad mini.

title: If you’re traveling in the Apple ecosystem, this is the tech you need to pack
content:
Macworld





One of the things I enjoy doing most with my family is traveling. Annually, we go on two or three domestic trips (at least one of them to Hawaii to visit relatives). We try to go on a big international trip every 18 months or so—I went to South Africa in 2024, and I just got back from a trip to Iceland in August to see the eclipse. And I always take a lot of gear with me.
Every great trip requires planning, whether it’s an overnight stay an hour away from home or a grand vacation in a country I’ve never visited before. Besides all the travel logistics (that my wife handles), there’s the tech you need to bring, which is my responsibility in my household.
Over the years, I’ve figured out what tech I absolutely need to take with me. There’s an art to figuring out what to bring. You don’t want to overdo it, because you’ll end up lugging around stuff you aren’t using. But you don’t want to be left without that thing you absolutely need and don’t really have a means of obtaining that item where you are.
While I now rely on my iPhone for all the photos and videos I shoot, I need other items to ensure a successful and enjoyable trip. Here’s a list of the gear I bring with me on my trips. This is the stuff I almost always bring no matter where I’m going. Hopefully, you can use this list to help you figure out what you need to bring on your next trip. If you have suggestions, drop me a line at rloyola@macworld.com. (Note: Prices stated here are MSRPs, but Amazon often runs sales and discounts on many of them.)


iPhone 18 Pro Max

				
					

				
			
Foundry




There was a time when I would bring separate video and still cameras on every trip, but the iPhone has gotten so good, I don’t need any other camera. With some practice and knowledge of iOS’s features and settings, or with third-party camera apps, you can replicate the capabilities of cameras that cost hundreds more. I just took a trip this past weekend and relied on the iPhone 18 Pro Max to document everything, but prior to this trip, I was using a iPhone 17 Pro Max, And before that, I used an iPhone 16 Plus, but I really prefer to the Pro’s telephoto lens.
$1299 at  Apple						
					
Learn more about the iPhone 17 Pro at Apple


							


MacBook Neo

				
					

				
			
Eugen Wegmann




On longer trips where I’ll shoot a lot of photos and video, I bring a MacBook so I can browse and manage my shots after each day is done. I used to bring an extremely old MacBook Pro instead of the MacBook Pro that I use daily, so if it was lost, stolen, or damaged on the trip, I wouldn’t sweat it that much. But it’s also extremely slow and heavy. Even with a recent $100 price hike, the MacBook Neo is such a delight–lightweight, fast, and durable. And as I point out in my review, it doesn’t need to be a secondary machine—the Neo is extremely capable of being a daily-use Mac.
$689 at  Amazon										 | 
																$689 at  B&H										 | 
																$699 at  Apple						
					
MacBook Neo on Amazon


							


Saily for international eSIMs

				
					

				
			
Foundry




My carrier offers international connectivity by partnering with carriers in other countries. I’ve mostly had success with it, but sometimes there are gaps in coverage or the speeds are slow. On my last trip abroad, I tried a different approach: I took advantage of the iPhone’s dual eSIM and used Saily to get a second eSIM for the country I was visiting. With a second eSIM, I switched between it and my carrier’s offering to get the best possible connection. Overseas eSIMs are affordable–sometimes they’re really cheap, making it worth a try. Learn more about using an eSIM when traveling and about using two eSIMs in an iPhone.
Saily in the App Store


							


Anker Nano Travel Adapter

				
					

				
			
Foundry




More and more hotels, especially those that cater to international clientele, are starting to install wall outlets that can be used with different types of power plugs. Hotels are also starting to have USB charging ports next to those wall outlets. But they’re not everywhere, so when you travel outside of the country, it’s good to have a power outlet adapter. The Anker Nano Travel Adapter ($20 during Amazon Prime Day) works in over 200 countries (it is not a voltage converter), and it can charge five devices at once.
Anker Nano Travel Adapter on Amazon


							


Coiled USB Charging Cables

				
					

				
			
Cable Matters




I try to rely on wireless connectivity/charging when I travel, but at some point, a cable is needed. I like bringing coiled cables because I find them easier to manage, especially when I have to connect a few phones for several people in my travel party who need to charge. I have a USB-C cable ($16.49 two-pack), but I also pack a USB-A to USB-C cable ($14.99 two-pack) because often planes don’t have USB-C ports. And I pack a USB-A to Lightning cable ($16 two-pack), because people I travel with have older iPhones.
Coiled USB-C Cable on Amazon
Coiled USB-A to USB-C Cable on Amazon
Coiled USB to Lighting Cable on Amazon


							


UGreen Nexode 65W GaN USB C Wall Charger

				
					

				
			
Foundry




It’s not difficult to find smaller, more capable chargers than the ones Apple sells. The $40 UGreen Nexode 65W GaN USB-C Wall Charger can charge three devices at once. A Glacier Blue model is $25 during Amazon Prime Day. See more chargers in our USB-C charger guide.
UGreen Nexode 65W GaN USB C Wall Charger on Amazon


							


UGreen Nexode Power Bank 20000mAh 100W

				
					

				
			
Foundry




You know what sucks? When you’re on a transcontinental flight and the outlets near your seat don’t work. That’s one of the reasons why I got the UGreen Nexode Power Bank 20000mAh 100W power bank ($52 during Amazon Prime Day). I’ve used it countless times when I couldn’t find a working outlet. It has enough juice to charge a laptop, and its 72-watt-hour capacity falls under the airline limits, so you can take it on a plane. Check out Macworld’s best laptop power banks for MacBooks for more options.
UGreen Nexode Power Bank 20000mAh 100W on Amazon


							


UGreen Magnetic Power Bank

				
					

				
			
Ugreen




I keep a MagSafe battery with me when I’m out exploring, just in case. This $31 Ugreen model (I’m a fan, if you haven’t noticed) supports MagSafe and USB-C 20W charging, but I mostly stick it to the back of my iPhone with MagSafe. Read Macworld’s best picks for magnetic power banks and MagSafe portable chargers for iPhone if you want something with more juice.
UGreen Magnetic Power Bank on Amazon


							


Apple AirPods Pro 

				
					

				
			
Andreas Bergsman




I prefer the AirPods Pro 3 ($179 during Amazon Prime Day) over the $149 AirPods 5 because the Pro’s in-ear fit seals out more noise and makes for a more comfortable trip on an airplane. AirPods go on sale often on Amazon, so look out for discounted prices. You can check out our AirPods Pro 3 review for in-depth testing, but you already know how great they are.
$179 at  Amazon										 | 
																$229 at  Best Buy US										 | 
																$229.99 at  B&H						
					
Apple AirPods Pro 3 on Amazon


							


Sony MDR-EX15LP wired earphones

				
					

				
			
Sony




I usually watch something on my iPhone during long flights, but sometimes the in-flight entertainment has something good. When I can, I plug in my own wired earphones to the airplane’s jack–I only use the ones the airline provides if the plane uses a two-prong audio jack. These Sony earphones with a 3.5mm connector are decent for the price ($10 on Amazon), and if I lose them, it’s not a big deal. 


						

							


Moft Trackable Snap-on Phone Stand & Wallet

				
					

				
			
Moft




This $50 wallet doubles as a stand–one item to carry instead of two? Say less. It is also trackable with the Find My app, which I haven’t had to resort to, thankfully, but is very nice to have and props up the iPhone at a perfect angle for watching videos. Plus, this wallet holds two cards, just enough for an ID and a hotel room key.
Moft Trackable Snap-on Phone Stand & Wallet on Amazon


							


Scosche WatchIt Keychain

				
					

				
			
Scosche




I’m not good about remembering to wear my Apple Watch every day, but I always take it when I travel, mostly because I use its remote trigger for the iPhone camera. I like this Apple Watch charger ($29 during Amazon Prime Day) because it’s small, even though the built-in USB-C port makes connecting it to a charger kind of tricky. But you can easily connect it to an iPhone or MacBook for a quick fill-up. See our other best Apple Watch Charger recommendations.
Scosche WatchIt Keychain on Amazon


							


Pelican PX18 Aegis Backpack

				
					

				
			
Pelican




I actually use an older Pelican backpack–it’s been with me for over 10 years now, and it’s the most durable backpack I’ve ever owned. But Pelican no longer makes it, and I’m eyeing the $200 Aegis to eventually replace it (if it ever wears out). It’s also available in a bigger 25-liter model. See Macworld’s best picks for MacBook backpacks, bags, cases and sleeves.
Pelican PX18 Aegis Backpack


							


Lee Men’s Extreme Motion Canvas Cargo Pant





				
					

				
			
Lee




Before you write to me that Macworld isn’t in a position to give fashion advice, let me be clear: These pants are practical, not fashionable. Cargo pants are ideal for carrying the things I need while seeing the sites. No, I’m not wearing them to a formal dinner. I’m not that gauche. These $42 Lee cargo pants are comfortable, and they don’t have the cargo pocket flaps that I find get in the way.
Lee Men's Extreme Motion Canvas Cargo Pant

title: Child-safety policy puts Apple & Brussels on unusually similar ground
content:
Apple Executive Chairman Tim Cook has praised the European Union's push for a common child-safety framework, giving Apple a rare point of agreement with regulators it has repeatedly fought over other technology rules.

Tim Cook and Ursula von der Leyen. Image source: Ursula von der Leyen on X
Cook made the comments during a visit to Strasbourg, where he met European Parliament President Roberta Metsola and lawmakers working on children's online safety.
He welcomed the European Parliament's effort to create a "harmonized, Europe-wide framework to keep kids safe." Cook said Apple was encouraged by the discussion surrounding the proposed EU KIDS Act.
The comments don't amount to an endorsement of every provision in the proposed law. They do show that Apple supports the EU's broader effort to establish a common approach to protecting children online across its member states.

title: 12 New Things to Expect From Apple in October
content:
October is about to become a very busy month for Apple, with the company set to release the iPhone Duo, both iOS 27.1 and iOS 27.2, and a new Mac Studio configuration with 512GB of RAM. In addition, up to seven more Apple products may be unveiled this month, including an all-new smart home hub, a new Apple TV 4K, a new HomePod mini, an iPad mini with an OLED display, MacBook Pro models with OLED displays, and more.


Below, we have outlined 12 new things to expect from Apple in October. This article was published previously and updated today to reflect the latest rumors.

Confirmed


iPhone Duo: The foldable iPhone Duo launches on Friday, October 23. Pre-orders begin Friday, October 16 at 5 a.m. Pacific Time.

  
iOS 27.1: Apple said the iPhone Duo will ship with iOS 27.1, so the software update is expected to be released before October 23.

  
iOS 27.2: Apple jumped ahead to an iOS 27.2 beta because iOS 27.1 is dedicated to the iPhone Duo. iOS 27.2 adds support for the five additional Siri AI languages that Apple promised would be coming in October, so accordingly we can expect iOS 27.2 to be released at some point during the month.

  
Mac Studio (512GB RAM): While the new Mac Studio with M5 Max and M5 Ultra chips was released last week, Apple said a high-end configuration with  the M5 Ultra and 512GB of RAM will be available in "late October."



Rumored


on Tuesday, October 13, according to a report from Bloomberg's Mark Gurman:
Home hub: An all-new Apple smart home hub featuring Siri AI, a 6-inch to 7-inch square display, an A18 chip or newer for Apple Intelligence, FaceTime, and more. A new operating system will feature clock faces, widgets, and more. There will be a tabletop version with a speaker base and a wall-mounted version.
↳ homeOS: Apple's smart home hub is expected to run an all-new operating system that may be named homeOS, according to trademark filings.

Apple TV 4K (4th Generation): A19 or A19 Pro chip, an increased 8GB to 12GB of RAM for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI support, an Apple-designed N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7 support, and an updated Siri Remote. A leak revealed the new Apple TV will look the same as the existing model.

HomePod mini 2: Newer chip, Siri AI support, improved sound quality, Apple's N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7 support, a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip, and new color options, including pink and green. No major design changes.
Apple is planning to unveil a second set of new products in the final week of October, according to MacRumors sources. While we do not know exactly which products are coming at this time, it is likely that the following Macs will be announced:
14" and 16" MacBook Pro models with OLED displays: A major MacBook Pro redesign with an OLED display, touchscreen support, M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, a Dynamic Island, a thinner-and-lighter design, and potentially Apple's C1X or C2 modem for built-in cellular connectivity.

24" iMac: M6 chip and new color options.

14" MacBook Pro: M6 chip.
A new iPad mini is also expected at some point in October:
iPad mini 8: OLED display, A20 Pro chip, landscape front camera, redesigned speaker system, and water-resistant design.
Apple has yet to announce an October event. When it held a "Scary Fast" event on October 30, 2023, Apple sent out invites six days prior, on October 24. Today is six days before the October 13 date that Apple reportedly plans to unveil an all-new home hub, so we shall see if history repeats itself and invites go out today.

title: Apple is reportedly set to launch a trio of smart home gadgets with LG
content:
Macworld





Pretty much the entire industry expects Apple to announce a HomePad speaker/screen hub next week, but a new report sheds light on the other products which will form part of the company’s imminent smart-home push.
Writing for Bloomberg, Mark Gurman says Apple’s October 13 announcements will also include a doorbell, a lock, a thermostat, and a range of security cameras, all developed in partnership with LG. He cites insider sources “who asked not to be identified because the undertaking is private” as well as regulatory filings which reveal “product names, specifications, features and drawings” of the devices. (These filings don’t mention Apple, however.)
While these products will reportedly be revealed next week, Gurman is pessimistic about the launch timeline. “Development of the LG accessories has lagged behind Apple’s own devices,” he warns, “and the products aren’t expected to reach consumers for at least a few more months.”
It isn’t just Gurman who expects these accessories to be unveiled soon. X leaker itspdfu has posted a thread of animated images of the devices, along with the following info:
LG Smart Deadbolt Lock: Keypad rotates to open. Features settings for Touchpad Light Ring, Door Left Audio Alarm, and Lock Sound Volume. Supports automatic unlocking, tap to unlock, emergency power, and master codes.
LG Smart Thermostat: Settings for Far Sight Display, Humidity Display, Brightness, Language.
LG Temperature Sensor: Temperature and humidity sensing. The sensor has a magnetic back to attach to metal surfaces. Comes with a metal plate with adhesive for attaching to other surfaces.
Combined with the hub, these products would form an entire ecosystem of quasi-first-party smart-home devices for Apple fans, with the only obvious gap in the mooted range being some form of smart bulb. Since the days of iOS 8 in 2014, the company has promoted its HomeKit framework, which enables a wide range of third-party products (many of which are sold on the Apple website) to operate with the Apple Home system and be easily controlled via an iPhone or iPad. But the quality and intuitiveness of these products have varied, and Apple may feel that having closer control over the hardware may help the devices win broader acceptance among the faithful.
It’s worth noting, however, that Apple is not expected to brand these products with its logo and name. They will, according to Gurman’s sources, carry the LG brand. (That company is also handling manufacturing and support for the products.) Gurman refers to this as a “second-party” supplier arrangement, and insists that the rumored Apple-branded accessories are still in the works.
Aside from the smart hub and the LG accessories, the company is expected to unveil a new Apple TV and HomePod mini on or about October 13. Then additional new products, likely focusing on the Mac and potentially including the iPad, are rumoured to arrive later this month.

				
					

				
			The LG Smart Deadbolt Lock is one of the “second-party” products expected to be announced next week.

title: Apple's escalating crackdown on ad vendors is catching some innocent victims
content:
When iOS 27 was released, a legit advertising company found it could no longer serve ads to the Safari browser. This block appears to be a mistake on Apple's side, but the ad industry is up in arms about the implications.


At least one ad agency was initially blocked in Safari when iOS 27 was launched.
Apple introduced App Tracking Transparency back in 2021 in order that users had to choose to allow ad companies to track them using identifiers. After a heavy initial impact, though, the rates of users allowing tracking has risen again, and advertisers have found alternative ways to learn about users.
However, according to advertising trade journal AdExchanger, The Trade Desk ad agency was blocked in iOS 27 by Apple itself. It appears that Apple is intentionally blocking data brokers who sell on tracked data, but in doing so it prevented The Trade Desk serving ads.

title: First Look at LG's Smart Home Products Made With Apple
content:
FCC filings reveal the designs of three upcoming LG smart home accessories that Apple reportedly helped develop, including a thermostat, a temperature sensor, and a deadbolt lock.


Yesterday, Bloomberg reported that Apple is working with LG Electronics on accessories for its upcoming home hub and other home products, citing regulatory documents without sharing the filings. FCC records MacRumors found contain label-placement drawings, three-dimensional renderings, and technical reports, providing a first look at the products' housings and additional details about their capabilities. 

smart thermostat, model TMCTAW5W, has a round, puck-like body with a raised edge. The drawing shows its back, with a small socket near the center and two round bumps near the bottom. Its specifications list a 24-volt AC power supply.


The Matter logo and QR setup code sit in the middle of the back, with regulatory text printed in a circle around them. A separate drawing shows the wiring connections arranged in two curved rows, with one on each side. LG's logo appears in the printing instructions.

radio test report also confirms a built-in 60 GHz radar. This could enable presence or approach detection.

pdfu," the thermostat offers a "Far Sight Display" setting, an option to display humidity, and controls for screen brightness and language. The leaker also lists temperature calibration and temperature offset settings, allowing users to adjust its temperature readings.

temperature sensor, model TMST2A6W, is also round and runs on a 3-volt CR2477 coin battery. On its back, the product name, model number, and manufacturing information curve around the outer edge.

test report confirms Bluetooth Low Energy and Thread connectivity.


The temperature sensor measures both temperature and humidity, according to pdfu. Its magnetic back allows it to attach directly to metal surfaces, while an included metal plate with adhesive enables mounting on other surfaces. The sensor's battery is replaceable, and it provides alerts when a replacement is needed.

smart deadbolt lock has a tall interior unit with straight sides and curved top and bottom ends. The filings reveal Graphite and Silver versions of the device, with model numbers TMCDD15G and TMCDD15S, respectively.

It runs on four AA batteries, which sit vertically side by side in a compartment in the upper half. Below them, a large, rotating circular section takes up almost the full width of the lower half. The Matter setup code and regulatory text sit above the battery compartment, near the top of the unit. 


The lock supports Bluetooth, Thread, near-field communication, and ultra wideband (UWB). An accompanying FCC order explains that it first verifies a compatible device's access credentials over Bluetooth, then uses UWB to determine its position before granting access. This provides more detail about the proximity-based automatic unlocking described in yesterday's report.

pdfu, the lock's keypad rotates open, with an included swivel pin allowing movement to be restricted on one side to prevent it from hitting a nearby wall. Its settings include controls for the touchpad's light ring, a "Door Left Audio Alarm," and lock sound volume. The lock also reportedly supports automatic unlocking, tap to unlock, emergency power, and master codes, comes with two mechanical keys, and fits 2.375-inch (60.3 mm) and 2.75-inch (69.9 mm) brackets.

title: EU Big Tech tax hike faces opposition not just from US, but at home too
content:
The European Union is considering a tax increase on Big Tech that it weirdly believes will avoid a US backlash, but on top of that, some EU members are already against it.


The EU is looking for tax income for its 2028-2034 budget from US Big Tech - image credit: EU
Back in July 2025, the European Union dropped its plans for a tax on Big Tech firms, seemingly as part of a move to appease Trump during trade negotiations. Now according to the Financial Times, the EU has a new plan that would raise similar sums without specifically being a digital tax.
Instead of targeting only digital firms, the EU proposes a levy on all companies over a certain size. At present, the proposal is for firms with annual revenues of around $117 million (100 million Euros) in the region.

title: Apple Reportedly Waiting on Samsung for Ultimate Bezel-Free iPhone Display
content:
Apple is waiting on Samsung to perfect a next-generation OLED display technology that wraps almost vertically around a phone and essentially makes the sides themselves part of the screen, claims a Chinese leaker.

Xiaomi's 2021 concept phone – bearing a striking resemblance to Samsung's rumored technology

According to the Weibo-based leaker Instant Digital, the technology is internally described by Samsung as a "full-surround, full-screen display." In the design – unlike a curved so-called "waterfall screen" – the main display remains completely flat, while the OLED panel bends sharply downward at close to a 90-degree angle on all four edges and corners.

The idea is that those folded display sections would effectively become the sides of the device and replace the typical metal or plastic frame. Meanwhile, the display wiring and other components usually hidden behind the bezels could also be moved around the edges.

The result – in theory – would be an iPhone that looks almost entirely bezel-free when viewed from the front, with the physical black border around the display reduced virtually to nothing. The technology could also reportedly facilitate an iPhone model without conventional mechanical buttons.

According to the leaker, Apple has been waiting for Samsung to finalize the technology, but there are still challenges to overcome. These are said to include optical distortion and color shifts around the corners, maintaining the OLED's protective encapsulation through extreme bends, and finding suitable locations for antennas when all sides are covered by the display.

Concept design shared by Instant Digital

The technology is quite different from the less-extreme "four-sided quad-curved display" that is rumored for Apple's 20th-anniversary iPhone expected in 2027. Indeed, the leaker suggests that the commemorative iPhone 20 model could be an intermediate step toward this more ambitious design. We'll see.

If you’re planning to buy a new iPhone, timing your purchase can save you hundreds of dollars or pounds. There are certain times of year when buying is a bad idea, and others when discounts, trade-in deals and retailer promotions make it much easier to get a bargain.
Apple rarely discounts its newest iPhones directly, but prices often fall after new models launch in September and during major sales events such as Black Friday. In 2026, however, the usual pattern changed: Apple raised prices across the range, with even 2025’s iPhone 17 increasing by £100 and the older iPhone 16 returning to its original price. So if your priority is getting the lowest possible price on the newest handset, right now may not be the best time to buy.
That doesn’t mean you should automatically wait. Whether it makes sense to buy now depends on which iPhone you’re considering. Some models, including the iPhone 17, 17e and Air, are still months away from replacement, while discontinued models such as the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max can see attractive prices as retailers clear remaining stock.
In this guide, we explain the best and worst times to buy an iPhone, whether now is a good time to buy each current model, when the best deals are likely to appear, and where to look for them. We’ll also cover whether it’s worth waiting for the next generation and when Apple typically cuts prices on older iPhones.

The worst time to buy an iPhone
This is generally in the weeks leading up to Apple’s September launch event, or in the early spring, when new models are expected to be announced. Buying just before a refresh means you could miss out on new features or pay full price for a model that’s about to be superseded.
The best time to buy an iPhone 
This depends on where you live:
In the U.K., where most iPhones are sold unlocked and off contract, the biggest savings are typically available during major sales events such as Amazon Prime Day (usually in July and October, and occasionally in March) and Black Friday in late November. However, worthwhile iPhone discounts can be found throughout the year if you know where to look.
In the U.S., where people tend to buy iPhones through a carrier, the best time to upgrade is often during Black Friday when networks enhance their offers with larger trade-in values, bill credits, gift cards, or discounted service plans. 


						

							







Should you buy a new iPhone now or wait? 

				
					

				
			
Ida Blix




September and the months that follow are a much better time to buy an iPhone than earlier in the summer. July and August are usually poor months to buy a Pro iPhone because Apple’s September launch is so close. The iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo have now been unveiled, removing that uncertainty.
If you need a phone now, there’s little reason to wait for another annual refresh, and the iPhone 17, 17e and Air are also relatively safe purchases because their successors aren’t expected until spring 2027. See: iPhone 18 and 18e rumors and iPhone Air 2 rumors. 
The iPhone 17 remains the strongest value, with a 120Hz ProMotion display, A19 chip, dual 48MP cameras and 256GB of storage for $899/£899 (although it was previously $799/£799). The 18 Pro and Pro Max make more sense if you want the best cameras, performance or battery life, while the Duo is for buyers specifically interested in Apple’s new folding design.
There is, however, one important reason to wait: 2027 could bring a much bigger iPhone redesign. Apple is rumored to be preparing a 20th-anniversary iPhone with a near-all-screen curved design, under-display Face ID, possible solid-state buttons, a thinner and more efficient OLED display, larger battery and major camera improvements. That could make 2027 a more significant upgrade year than 2026.
So if your current iPhone is still serving you well, waiting could be worthwhile. Otherwise, buy now if you need a phone, or wait until Black Friday if price is your main concern.

When does Apple release new iPhones?
Apple has a well-established pattern of releasing new iPhones every year, typically in September. This annual cycle has been remarkably consistent for over a decade, with only rare exceptions. 
While September remains the anchor for high-end models, Apple has begun to stagger its iPhone launches. Starting with the iPhone 16e in early 2025 and continuing with the iPhone 17e in spring 2026, Apple now releases more affordable models at separate events earlier in the year – often in March. 
The iPhone 18 lineup is expected to take this strategy a step further. In September 2026 Apple launched the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, alongside the foldable iPhone Duo. The standard iPhone 18, iPhone 18e, and iPhone Air 2 are expected to follow in spring 2027.
September launches are usually accompanied by a dedicated Apple keynote, while spring releases are more likely to be announced via a press release although Apple has held spring events. Following the announcement, Apple typically opens pre-orders within a few days, with devices going on sale one to two weeks later. Initial availability can be limited, particularly for the most popular models and storage configurations.


						

							


Should you wait for the iPhone 18?
For most people, there isn’t a strong reason to wait for the iPhone 18. Apple isn’t expected to launch the standard model until spring 2027, so buying an iPhone 17 before the end of 2026 would still give you several months with Apple’s current mainstream model before its replacement arrives.
The iPhone 18 is expected to bring a 2nm A20 chip, potentially 9GB or 12GB of RAM, Apple’s C2 modem and possibly a new 24MP front camera. Extra RAM could prove particularly useful for future Apple Intelligence and Siri features. However, the rear camera system is still expected to consist of two 48MP cameras, while the display may remain broadly similar to the iPhone 17’s 6.3-inch ProMotion panel.
There is also some uncertainty over exactly what the iPhone 18 lineup will look like. A September 2026 rumour suggested Apple could effectively merge the standard iPhone and iPhone Air into a single model, rather than continuing them as two separate devices. If that happens, the iPhone 18 could adopt some of the Air’s thinner, lighter design while retaining the broader appeal of the standard iPhone. For now, though, that remains speculative.
Price is another consideration. With the arrival of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo, Apple increased iPhone prices across the range, so the iPhone 17 now costs $899, $100 more than at launch. When the iPhone 18 arrives, it is likely to inherit that $899 price point, while the iPhone 17 could drop back to around $799 at which you may regret buying it at the higher price.
Wait if you want the newer A20 chip, potentially more RAM, an improved front camera, or are intrigued by the possibility of a thinner redesigned standard model. 
Don’t wait if you simply want ProMotion, dual 48MP cameras, excellent battery life and 256GB of storage as standard – the iPhone 17 already delivers all of that.

 FAQ 


1.
When is the best carrier upgrade timing? 
Apple typically announces new iPhone models in September. Carriers often roll out their most aggressive trade-in offers and promotional deals around this time to entice customers to upgrade.
New releases: Waiting for the September (or spring) launch window is generally a good strategy if you want the latest model at a potentially better subsidized price.
Check your contract cycle: Many carrier contracts today last 24 to 36 months. If you’re nearing the end of your contract, you’re in a strong position to negotiate or take advantage of upgrade offers. However, upgrading mid-contract may involve paying off the remaining balance, so it’s worth checking your specific terms.
Consider Apple’s upgrade plans: Apple has replaced its old iPhone Upgrade Program with newer financing and leasing options. In the U.S., Apple Upgrade lets you lease an iPhone through Klarna and upgrade, buy or return it at the end of the term. In the U.K., Apple’s Flexible Finance Account offers eligible iPhones on monthly payment plans with the option to upgrade after a set number of payments. Terms and monthly costs vary by model.





2.
When does Apple update the iPhone?
Apple follows a well-established annual rhythm for its iPhone updates, with the primary event taking place in September each year. 
Apple typically unveils its new iPhone lineup at a dedicated Apple Event in September. Pre-orders usually open on the Friday following the announcement, with devices shipping and arriving in stores a week later. 
Apple also occasionally introduces new iPhones outside the September window and in the past it has held a Spring Apple Event at which more affordable iPhones have launched. The iPhone 17e, for example, arrived in March 2026, and the iPhone 16e launched in February 2025. 
Compatible iPhone models also get a yearly operating system software update with new features that can make your old iPhone feel new again. The major iOS updates follow the September schedule.
Read our guide to the next Apple event to find out if an Apple event is imminent.





3.
When do iPhone prices drop and by how much?
Based on past experience, Apple is very unlikely to reduce the price of a new iPhone during its first year on sale.
However, when Apple introduces a new generation of iPhones, it usually cuts the price of the previous year’s models. That means September has traditionally been the point when older iPhones become cheaper.
Apple also tends to keep launch prices broadly similar from one generation to the next, at least in the U.S., although exchange rates and other regional factors can affect pricing elsewhere.
In 2024, for example, Apple reduced the price of the iPhone 15 and iPhone 15 Plus by $100/£100 when the iPhone 16 and 16 Plus arrived. The iPhone 16 also fell in price following the launch of the iPhone 17 in 2025. However, because the iPhone 17 doubled the base storage to 256GB, the older iPhone 16 looked less attractive even at $100/£100 less.
In 2026, the pattern changed. Apple actually raised iPhone prices, blaming higher memory costs. Even the year-old iPhone 17 and two-year-old iPhone 16 increased by $100, showing that older iPhones don’t always become cheaper when a new generation arrives.





4.
Is it better to buy from Apple or a carrier?
In the U.S., buying from Apple is usually the better option if you value flexibility. If you pay in full or use Apple’s own financing, the iPhone is unlocked, so you can switch carriers or use another eSIM when traveling. Apple also accepts trade-ins and, importantly, many AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon promotions are available when buying through Apple.
However, an iPhone bought from Apple but financed through an AT&T, T-Mobile or Verizon device-payment plan is locked to that carrier until it has been paid off. An iPhone bought outright from Apple isn’t.
The main reason to buy directly from AT&T, T-Mobile or Verizon is to take advantage of a particularly good promotion. U.S. carriers frequently advertise large trade-in credits or “free” iPhones, especially when you add a line or switch networks. The catch is that the discount is usually provided as monthly bill credits over 24 or 36 months, so if you leave early you can lose the remaining credits.
In the U.K., Apple sells iPhones unlocked and SIM-free, allowing you to shop separately for a SIM-only plan from EE, Vodafone, O2, Three or an MVNO. This makes it easier to switch networks and can work out cheaper over the life of the phone than bundling the handset and airtime into a single contract.
Apple isn’t necessarily the cheapest place to buy, however. Amazon U.K. and other retailers frequently discount SIM-free iPhones, and there can be substantial savings during sales events such as Black Friday.
Networks can also offer compelling promotions, including enhanced trade-in values, discounted airtime, generous data allowances or lower monthly payments. But make sure you compare the total cost of the contract, rather than focusing on the headline monthly price.





5.
When are the best iPhone deals?
The earliest you could expect to get a discount on the newest iPhones is around Black Friday at the end of November, so you might be planning to hold out until then. However, the deals we tend to see, if any, are usually for older handsets. See our round-up of Best Black Friday iPhone deals for more.
Nor should you expect to get a discount in an Apple Black Friday sale. Apple’s Black Friday sale usually only takes the form of vouchers with select product purchases, rather than a discount, and it is unlikely that the newest iPhone would qualify as in previous year’s new iPhones haven’t been included. 
Note that while shopping events like Black Friday get all the attention, that’s not the only time you can get discounts on Apple products: we see discounts all the time. Another event where we see good iPhone deals is Prime Day, which happens in June or July and October every year. So take a look at the iPhone deals for Amazon Prime Day sale to see what you might be able to save.
In our experience, we don’t tend to see discounts on the newest handset until the spring – and these are always from third-party resellers, never from Apple. In fact, we don’t tend to see the iPhone discounted in the U.S. very often, most of the discounts we see are in the U.K. where unlocked iPhones are often sold off-contract at a good discount.





6.
Is it worth buying a refurbished iPhone? 
Yes, buying a refurbished iPhone is absolutely worth it for most people, especially if you want to save money without sacrificing quality. 
Buying refurbished is a great way to “pick up a bargain” while still getting a premium device. You can typically save 15% to 30% compared to buying new, and sometimes much more on older models. 
A common misconception is that refurbished is the same as buying a used phone from a stranger, though. It’s not. A used phone is sold “as-is,” with no guarantee it will work properly. A refurbished phone has been professionally inspected, tested, and repaired if needed, and it comes with a warranty. 
If you want the highest quality, Apple’s own refurbished store is the gold standard.





Conclusion: When is the best time to buy a new iPhone?
The worst time to buy is usually between July or August, mainly because with new iPhones on the horizon the price of the older handsets are likely to drop very soon.
If you want the newest iPhones then the best deals don’t tend to come before the spring and summer months. If you are happy to buy an older iPhone then you will probably see decent deals around Prime Day and Black Friday – but deals happen all year round. 
We hope this article has proved helpful in reaching an informed buying decision. Remember that good prices can be found all year round, if a retailer is feeling generous and you know where to look: read our guide to the best iPhone deals for more on that.

The good news is that Apple Watch pricing has remained largely unchanged, while the AirPods 5 launched at a lower price. And across the board, Prime Day should still be one of the best opportunities to buy Apple products for less than Apple charges.

At Macworld, we’ve been covering and reviewing Apple and Apple devices for more than four decades, from the original Macintosh to the latest Macs, iPhones, iPads, AirPods and Apple Watches. We use Apple products every day and purchase them with our own money, so we know a good deal when we see one.

title: Apple's Own Home Security Camera Still Coming Next Year
content:
Apple's home security camera remains in development separately from the LG-made accessories reported yesterday, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman has clarified. In a follow-up post on X, Gurman said the security cameras co-developed with LG are "completely separate" from Apple's privacy-centric home camera and sensor, which he says is still coming next year.

reported previously, Apple's device will not record video, using AI instead to analyze the home environment and detect which room a person is in. Bloomberg first reported a 2027 home security system and service in September. The LG-branded lineup spans a video doorbell, deadbolt lock, thermostat and indoor and outdoor cameras, and is not expected for at least a few more months.

Amazon’s October Prime Day sale is one of the best opportunities this year to buy an iPad for less, and it ends today, October 7.
That matters more than usual in 2026 because Apple raised iPad prices substantially in June. The standard iPad now starts at $449/£429, the iPad mini at $599/£599, the 11-inch iPad Air at $749/£749, and the 11-inch iPad Pro at $1,199/£1,199. Retailer discounts can therefore save hundreds compared with buying directly from Apple.
But not every iPad deal will be worth grabbing. The M4 iPad Air and M5 iPad Pro are both relatively recent models and aren’t expected to be replaced until 2027, making a strong Prime Day discount easy to recommend.
The situation is different for the iPad mini. Apple is widely expected to introduce a new model soon, potentially before the end of October, with an OLED display among the biggest rumored upgrades. And while the current A16 iPad probably won’t be replaced until early 2027, it remains the only iPad Apple sells that doesn’t support Apple Intelligence.
Below, we’re tracking the best October Prime Day iPad deals and explaining which discounts are genuinely worth taking and which models you may be better off waiting for. Of course, Prime Day isn’t just for iPads. If you’re looking for a new Mac, Apple Watch, or set of AirPods, check out our big roundup of the Best Apple Prime Day Deals.

Apple




The A16 iPad remains Apple’s cheapest tablet, but Apple raised its price by $100/£100 in June, and it is the only current iPad without Apple Intelligence.
A new iPad is expected later in 2026 or in early 2027, likely with a newer processor, more RAM and Apple Intelligence support, so we wouldn’t recommend paying close to the current $449/£429 price.

October is now the leading launch window for the next iPad mini, with reports pointing to an OLED display and newer processor.

The M4 iPad Air is the best choice for most people and probably the safest Prime Day buy. It offers considerably more performance than the standard iPad without the expense of the Pro, comes in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes, and isn’t expected to be replaced until 2027.
iPad Pro: Best for professionals/creative users
The M5 iPad Pro is aimed at demanding creative and professional users who will benefit from its performance and OLED display. It’s also safe to buy this Prime Day, but most people will get better value from the iPad Air.
For more advice read our guide to the Best iPad.


						

							


Prime Day iPad deals to avoid

				
					

				
			
Dominik Tomaszewski / Foundry




When deciding whether to shop for an iPad deal, we recommend you keep a few things in mind:
If you’re considering an iPad as a laptop replacement, remember to factor in the price of a keyboard. Adding an Apple keyboard case can add hundreds to the cost and, depending on the iPad, push the total close to or above the price of a MacBook. The arrival of the lower-cost MacBook Neo makes that comparison even more important.
Be particularly cautious about iPad mini deals. The current A17 Pro model could be replaced as soon as later in October, with an OLED display among the expected upgrades. Unless the Prime Day discount is substantial, you may be better off waiting.
The iPad (A16) is currently the only tablet in Apple’s active lineup that does not support Apple Intelligence. A replacement is expected in early 2027, so avoid paying close to Apple’s full price. A substantial discount, however, can still make the current model a good-value choice.
Deals on older or refurbished iPads can be tempting, but check software support before buying. iPadOS 27 drops support for several older models, so make sure the iPad you’re considering can run the current operating system.
Avoid paying extra for a Cellular model unless you truly need it. Cellular versions cost significantly more and may also require a monthly data plan. If you usually carry an iPhone, Personal Hotspot is often a cheaper alternative.
Casual users should also think twice before jumping on an iPad Pro (M5) deal. Unless you need its OLED display or additional performance for demanding creative and professional workflows, the M4 iPad Air offers better value for most people.
Likewise, don’t pay extra for the iPad Pro’s nano-texture glass unless you regularly work in bright or uncontrolled lighting.


						

							


Should you buy an iPad during Prime Day?
October Prime Day is one of the better times of the year to buy an iPad, particularly after Apple raised iPad prices substantially in June. Amazon’s October sale often comes close to Black Friday pricing, so a good deal could offset much of Apple’s price increase. 
The model you choose matters, though. The M4 iPad Air and M5 iPad Pro are relatively safe buys because neither is expected to be replaced until 2027. The A16 iPad can also be worth buying at a substantial discount, although it is the only current iPad without Apple Intelligence. We’d be much more cautious about the iPad mini, as a new model could arrive soon after Prime Day.
There are a few other things to consider before making a purchase:
Prime membership is required: Many of the best deals are exclusive to Amazon Prime members. If you’re not already subscribed, you might be able to take advantage of Amazon’s 30-day free trial or you could sign up for a month and cancel afterward. As well as getting free two-day shipping, Prime customers also get access to Prime Video and Music. Prime memberships cost $139 / £95 annually, or $14.99 / £8.99 / AU$6.99 every month. 
Other sales: If you miss Prime Day, you’ll have another chance to save during the Black Friday sales in November which historically brings some of the lowest iPad prices of the year.
Student Discounts: Students can save significantly through the Apple Education Store. For example, students can save $50/£50 on the iPad Air and $100/£100 on the iPad Pro when shopping at Apple’s U.S. Education Store or Apple’s U.K. Education Store.
Compare Prices: Amazon isn’t always the cheapest option. Retailers such as Walmart and Best Buy frequently run competing promotions around the time of Prime Day, so it’s worth comparing prices before buying.
Prime Day is available in multiple countries, including Australia, Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Canada, China, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, Mexico, the Netherlands, Portugal, Singapore, Spain, the U.K., and the U.S.


						

							


Why you can trust Macworld’s recommendations
The Prime Day iPad deals picked here are all chosen by our editors, who have decades of experience with Apple devices. We’ve reviewed everything we recommend, and we won’t tell you to buy something that’s not an actual deal. We track current prices against previous lows and only highlight discounts we think are worth considering. During Prime Day, we continually update this page as better deals appear, selecting the configurations that offer the best value for each product type. Apple products are expensive, so we focus on prices we’d be willing to pay ourselves—and deals we believe will genuinely save you money.


						

							




Prime Day 2026: More outstanding Apple deals
Throughout the Prime Day sale, we constantly check Amazon’s listings to find the best deals. We’ve tested all of the models we recommend here and compare current pricing with previous lows, Apple’s retail price and the age of the model before deciding whether a deal is genuinely worth considering.

Buy the Series 12 if you want Apple’s latest health features without the size and expense of the Ultra. It combines the new Health Sensing System with a 24-hour battery rating and starts at $399/£369.
Apple Watch Ultra 4: Best for endurance and outdoor use
Choose the Ultra 4 if you need 50-hour battery life, satellite connectivity, precision GPS, diving support or extended workout tracking.
Apple Watch SE 3: Best budget option
The SE 3 is the cheapest current Apple Watch and provides most of the core smartwatch, fitness and safety experience. Its main omissions are Apple’s more advanced health sensors.

Don’t automatically dismiss last year’s watches. If retailers heavily discount remaining stock, Series 11 and Ultra 3 can offer better value than the new models when the discount is large enough – as we’re already seeing on some U.K. configurations.

Don’t assume an older Apple Watch is a bad buy. The Series 11 and Ultra 3 are only one generation old and can make excellent buys if they’re substantially cheaper than the Series 12 or Ultra 4.
Be much more cautious with the Series 8, SE 2 and original Ultra, however. Those models cannot run watchOS 27. The Series 9 is the oldest standard Apple Watch compatible with watchOS 27, while the Ultra 2 is the oldest supported Ultra.
Also compare the sale price with the newest equivalent. A $50 Series 11 saving, for example, may not be enough to justify giving up the Series 12’s new health features, whereas a substantially larger saving could change the calculation.
Should you buy GPS or Cellular?
Don’t automatically pay extra for cellular. The Series 12 costs $100/£100 more with cellular, while the SE 3 premium is $50/£70. Cellular is included with every Ultra 4. For many users, GPS is sufficient because the Watch can still track workouts, use Apple Pay and play downloaded music without an iPhone. Cellular becomes most useful if you regularly leave your iPhone behind but still want calls, messages and online services. Read: Do I need a cellular Apple Watch?

It’s also an excellent time to look at previous-generation stock. Series 11 and Ultra 3 are still relatively recent watches, and retailers may discount them aggressively now that their replacements are available.
The other option is to wait until Black Friday in November. If an October deal is modest and you aren’t in a hurry, Black Friday may bring another opportunity – but there’s no guarantee that a particular configuration or older model will remain in stock. Which MacBook should you buy?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Apple’s current MacBook range falls into three clear categories:
MacBook Air M5: Best MacBook for most people
The M5 MacBook Air is our default recommendation for most buyers. It combines strong performance, long battery life and portability without the higher price of a MacBook Pro. With no replacement expected until 2027, a good Prime Day discount would be easy to recommend.
MacBook Neo: Best budget MacBook
The MacBook Neo is the cheapest MacBook and is best suited to students and anyone who mainly needs a laptop for web browsing, documents, streaming and video calls. If a discounted MacBook Air is only moderately more expensive, however, the Air is the better long-term buy.
MacBook Pro M5: Best for demanding work
The MacBook Pro is the better choice for video editing, software development, 3D work and other demanding tasks that benefit from sustained performance. Prime Day discounts could be worthwhile, although a touchscreen MacBook Pro is rumored for later in October.
MacBook Pro M5 Pro/Max: Best for professional workloads
Choose an M5 Pro or M5 Max model if you need significantly more CPU and GPU performance, additional memory or greater connectivity. If you already own an M4 Pro or M4 Max model, there is little reason to upgrade.
For most Prime Day shoppers, we recommend starting with the 13-inch M5 MacBook Air. The MacBook Neo becomes especially compelling when heavily discounted, while MacBook Pro buyers should consider whether they need the additional performance and professional features enough to justify the considerably higher price.

Should I buy a MacBook Neo?
Should I buy a MacBook Air?
Should I buy a MacBook Pro?


						

							


Which Mac desktop should you buy?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Mac mini M6: Best desktop for most people
The new M6 Mac mini is our default desktop recommendation. It starts at $899/£899 and is ideal for home offices, general productivity, coding, photo editing and less demanding creative work. Because it launched only in September, a significant Prime Day discount would be particularly attractive.
Mac mini M5 Pro: Best compact professional desktop
Choose the M5 Pro model if you need more CPU and GPU performance, Thunderbolt 5, greater memory bandwidth or more than 32GB of unified memory.
Mac Studio M5 Max: Best professional workstation
The M5 Max Mac Studio offers considerably greater GPU performance, more memory and more connectivity than the Mac mini and is our preferred Studio configuration for most professional users.
iMac: Best all-in-one
The M4 iMac remains the obvious choice if you want an integrated 4.5K display and minimal desk clutter, but its older M4 chip and $1,499/£1,499 starting price mean we’d only recommend it with a substantial discount.
For more advice read:
Should I buy a Mac mini?
Should I buy a Mac Studio?


						

							


Prime Day Mac & MacBook deals to avoid
The cheapest Mac isn’t always the best value. Rather than using Prime Day simply to spend less, use it as an opportunity to get better specifications for the same budget.
When buying a Mac in 2026, try to get as much RAM and storage as you can afford. Most current Macs now start with 16GB of unified memory, although some still have only 256GB of storage. The main exception for memory is the entry-level MacBook Neo, which has 8GB of RAM and a 256GB SSD.
Because Apple silicon Macs can’t have their unified memory or internal storage upgraded later, it’s worth buying enough for your future needs. Memory is particularly important for demanding creative work, development and AI workloads.
For most buyers, prioritizing memory will provide greater long-term benefits than paying extra for a faster processor. Professional users may want 36GB or more, while 64GB or more can be worthwhile for demanding video production, software development and AI workloads.
Don’t buy a MacBook Neo simply because it’s the cheapest Mac: If an M5 Air is only around $200/£200 more, the Air gives you 16GB RAM, better display support and considerably more headroom.
Don’t pay close to full price for an M4 Mac mini: It has now been replaced. Clearance is only attractive if the discount properly reflects that.
Don’t confuse M6 Mac mini with M5 Pro Mac mini: M6 is the mainstream chip; M5 Pro remains much faster for many professional workloads despite the apparently older number. Macworld
Don’t buy a MacBook Pro purely because the discount looks enormous: Apple increased MSRP dramatically in June, so a “$400 off” deal may simply bring it closer to what the machine cost before the increase. Compare the actual selling price with the historic lows in your table.


						

							


Should you buy a MacBook or Mac during Prime Day?
October Prime Day is a good opportunity to buy a Mac, but whether you should take a deal depends on the model.
The M5 MacBook Air is particularly easy to recommend because it is not expected to be replaced until 2027. The new M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini are also safe purchases from a product-cycle perspective, although their recent launch means discounts may initially be smaller.
MacBook Pro buyers have a more difficult decision. The current M5 models are powerful machines and a large discount may outweigh the benefit of waiting, but a touchscreen MacBook Pro is rumored for later in October.
MacBook Neo buyers should watch the price closely. The previous Prime Day low was $589.99/£549, so a deal near or below those figures would be especially attractive.
We’d avoid the iMac unless you find a substantial discount because of its age and relatively high starting price.
Finally, remember that Amazon isn’t the only retailer likely to cut prices during Prime Day. Best Buy, Walmart and B&H in the U.S., and retailers including Currys, John Lewis and others in the U.K., may run competing promotions, so compare prices before buying.
Before you buy, keep the following in mind:
Prime membership is required: Many of the best deals are exclusive to Amazon Prime members. If you’re not already subscribed, you might be able to take advantage of Amazon’s 30-day free trial or you could sign up for a month and cancel afterward. As well as getting free two-day shipping, Prime customers also get access to Prime Video and Music. Prime memberships cost $139 / £95 annually, or $14.99 / £8.99 / AU$6.99 every month. 
Other sales: If you miss Prime Day, you’ll have another chance to save during the Black Friday sales in November.
Student Discounts: Students can get discounts at Apple’s Education Store. See: Apple’s U.S. Education Store or Apple’s U.K. Education Store.
Prime Day is available in multiple countries, including Australia, Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Canada, China, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, Mexico, the Netherlands, Portugal, Singapore, Spain, the U.K., and the U.S.



						

							


Why you can trust Macworld’s recommendations
The MacBooks and Mac desktops featured here are selected by our editors, who have decades of experience with Apple devices. We compare current prices with previous lows and Apple’s retail prices, and we’ll tell you when a discount isn’t good enough rather than recommending a deal simply because it’s cheaper than MSRP. During Prime Day we continually update this page as better deals appear.

title: Formula 1 Coverage on Apple TV to Get Dolby Atmos Later This Month
content:
Formula 1 coverage on Apple TV is set to be broadcast in Dolby Atmos beginning later this month.


Starting with the U.S. Grand Prix weekend on Friday, October 23 in Austin, Texas, Formula 1 coverage on Apple TV will be available in Dolby Atmos on supported devices.

Apple says the introduction of Dolby Atmos will create a more immersive presentation designed to put viewers at the center of the race. The Atmos mix will encompass team radio, commentary, engines, on-track battles, and activity in the pit lane.

The combination of Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos is intended to capture the full audiovisual intensity of Formula 1 and bring viewers closer to the action, according to Apple.

The Hollywood Reporter about the new presentation:
"If you are a sports fan today, our viewpoint is that the experience is – I'm going to be polite and say not easy. There really has not been a lot of innovation. We went into sports a couple of years back with the intention to make a difference for the customer, and this is a continuation of that journey."
"The sound is what makes it emotional; it is the sound that guides you through that and builds the tension," said John Couling, senior VP of entertainment for Dolby Laboratories, speaking to THR. "That is what Dolby Atmos will deliver."

The Atmos presentation works on supported Apple devices and compatible Dolby-enabled TVs, soundbars, and home-theater systems.
 
announced a five-year partnership including exclusive streaming rights in the U.S. The partnership allows ‌Apple TV‌ to provide comprehensive coverage of Formula 1, including all practice, qualifying, Sprint sessions, and Grands Prix.
